newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major "furious" with Clarke on Europe.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major "furious" with Clarke on Europe.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major was reported to be furious with finance minister Kenneth Clarke on Tuesday after remarks by Clarke reopened a chasm over Europe that threatens irreparably to split the Conservative party.
Senior government sources were quoted by several newspapers as saying Major was "very angry" at Clarke's overt support for a single European currency.

Major's Downing Street office said it had no comment on the reports. But senior officials studiously avoided a defence of Clarke's remarks, saying only: "The prime minister has made clear that we have a settled policy which stands."

The government's official policy, which Major instigated to try and bridge the yawning divide between pro-Europeans and anti-Europeans in his party, is that it will decide what is in Britain's interests after the single currency is launched.

In an interview during a weekend meeting of European finance ministers in Ireland, Chancellor of the Exchequer Clarke said it would be "pathetic" for Britain to wait and see how a European single currency developed before deciding whether to join.

"That would be the worst policy of all of the British doing their traditional business of not be able to make their minds up and then joining late," said Clarke, seen as the most likely successor to Major from the party's left wing.
Clarke's remarks provoked strong pressure on Major from anti-Europeans to ditch Clarke, the most pro-European member of the cabinet, before an election due within eight months.

Major negotiated an "opt-out" from monetary union when negotiating the Maastricht treaty in 1991. Anti-Europeans want him to rule out entry into a single currency in the life of the next five-year parliament and want that pledge to be a commitment in the election manifesto.
Getting rid of Clarke would be an extremely risky manoeuvre.
Markets, who see him as a "safe pair of hands" and praise his careful management of the current economic upturn, would be dismayed at his sacrifice on the altar of political expediency.

Pro-Europeans would be outraged. They have begun fighting back against opponents they fear are dominating political debate and include senior party figures like former prime minister Edward Heath and a battery of former ministers.
The opposition Labour party is already 20 points ahead in opinion polls. Conservative strategists are worried the European issue will dominate their party conference in early October.

Home Secretary Michael Howard, a cabinet member hostile to European integration, used a BBC interview on crime figures on Tuesday to say government policy was unchanged. The opposition, he said, was soft on Europe.

But Howard heightened speculation over Clarke by carefully sidestepping a request to confirm or deny the rift between Clarke and Major, saying only: "I don't think you should believe everything you read in the newspapers."
Heath told the BBC the reports of Major's anger were part of an attempt by anti-Europeans to "stampede" the government into a tougher policy on the single currency.
Heath dismissed suggestions Clarke would quit, saying: "He won't leave the government... (I'm) quite confident because he knows he's done a splendid job and he will keep on doing it."
Right-wing newspapers openly speculated about Clarke's chances of survival. The Times said in an editorial: "Clarke... can go. He would be less missed than he would like to think and little mourned."
